title: REST vs RPC vs gRPC (and where tRPC and GraphQL fit)
objectives: Tell a resource-shaped API from a procedure-shaped one by its endpoints, and say what each gets from HTTP
Explain what gRPC adds — a `.proto` contract with generated clients, HTTP/2, four call types, deadlines — and why browsers need gRPC-Web and a translating proxy
Explain how tRPC v11 shares a contract without code generation, and what that requires of every client
Choose REST, gRPC, tRPC or GraphQL from who calls the API, and justify the choice

questions.prompt: An API has `POST /api/getInvoice`, `POST /api/sendInvoice` and `POST /api/voidInvoice`. What shape is it, and what does that cost?

options.text: Procedure-shaped: every call is a `POST`, so caches can't store the reads and generic clients can't tell reads from writes
REST — it's JSON over HTTP
Resource-shaped, because `invoice` is a noun in every URL
gRPC, because gRPC calls are always `POST`

questions.explanation: The URL names a function and the method is always `POST` — that's RPC over HTTP. It's a legitimate design, but `POST /api/getInvoice` isn't cacheable and isn't retried as idempotent the way `GET /invoices/42` is. "JSON over HTTP" says nothing about shape, and gRPC is a specific protocol (HTTP/2, protobuf, `application/grpc`), not any API that uses `POST`.

questions.prompt: A product catalogue is read millions of times a day through a CDN. Which endpoint can the CDN cache with standard HTTP rules and no extra machinery?

options.text: `GET /products/42`
`POST /rpc/getProduct` with `{"id":42}`
`POST /graphql` with a `product(id: 42)` query
A unary gRPC `GetProduct` call

questions.explanation: RFC 9110 makes `GET` responses cacheable by default; a cached `POST` response can at most answer a later `GET` of the same URL — never another `POST` (section 9.3.3). The RPC, GraphQL and gRPC variants all travel as `POST`s to URLs that don't identify the product, so caching them needs persisted queries, custom keys or an app-level cache. Public, read-heavy data is where resource-shaped HTTP earns its keep.

questions.prompt: A gRPC call fails with status `NOT_FOUND`. What HTTP status code does the response carry?

options.text: `200` — the gRPC status travels in the `grpc-status` trailer
`404`, mapped from `NOT_FOUND`
`500`, because any gRPC error is a server error at the HTTP layer
None — gRPC doesn't use HTTP

questions.explanation: gRPC rides on HTTP/2 but reports call outcomes in trailers: `grpc-status: 0` is OK, `5` is `NOT_FOUND`, and the HTTP status stays `200`. The gRPC protocol spec notes this is why a server should answer `415` to non-gRPC clients — so a plain HTTP/2 client doesn't read a gRPC error as success. Monitoring that counts HTTP `5xx`s sees none of these failures.

questions.prompt: Your React app wants to call an internal gRPC service directly from the browser. What does that take?

options.text: A gRPC-Web client plus something that translates it to gRPC (usually a proxy such as Envoy) — and only unary and server-streaming calls
Nothing special: browsers speak HTTP/2, and gRPC is HTTP/2
Just CORS headers on the gRPC server
A bidirectional stream over `fetch`, which replaces the proxy

questions.explanation: Browsers do use HTTP/2, but `fetch` exposes neither HTTP/2 framing nor trailers, so a page can't speak native gRPC. gRPC-Web is a browser-friendly variant that has to be translated — usually by a proxy such as Envoy (grpc-web's default), or by a server framework with gRPC-Web built in; per the grpc-web README it supports unary and server-streaming calls (the latter only in `grpcwebtext` mode), and client/bidirectional streaming are not supported. CORS may be needed on top, but it doesn't change the protocol.

questions.prompt: You delete `string note = 3;` from a protobuf message that deployed services still exchange. What should you do with the number 3?

options.text: Mark it `reserved` so no future field reuses it
Renumber the later fields down to close the gap
Nothing — protobuf matches fields by name
Reuse it for the next field you add, to keep numbers dense

questions.explanation: The field number identifies the field in the binary wire format and can't change once the message is in use. An old binary that still sends field 3 as a string would be misread if 3 came back as, say, an `int64 amount`. Renumbering breaks every deployed peer; names don't appear on the wire at all. The proto3 guide says you must reserve a deleted field's number.

questions.prompt: What does tRPC require that a REST + OpenAPI design doesn't?

options.text: Client and server in TypeScript, with the client able to import the server router's type (one repo or a shared package)
A schema file and a code-generation step
HTTP/2 between client and server
A GraphQL server underneath

questions.explanation: tRPC's contract *is* `typeof appRouter`, imported type-only by the client, so the TypeScript compiler is what checks calls — no schema, no generator, but also no use to a Swift app or a partner's Python script. On the wire it's ordinary HTTP: `GET` for queries, `POST` for mutations, JSON bodies. (tRPC v11 also requires TypeScript 5.7.2 or later.)

questions.prompt: A payments company has (a) a public API for merchants in many languages, (b) a dozen internal Go, Java and Python services that stream events to each other, and (c) its own Next.js dashboard backed by a TypeScript server in the same repo. Which mapping fits best?

options.text: (a) REST described with OpenAPI, (b) gRPC, (c) tRPC
tRPC everywhere — one style is simpler
gRPC everywhere, merchants included
(a) gRPC, (b) GraphQL, (c) REST

questions.explanation: Merchants have only HTTP libraries and your docs, so a resource-shaped API with a language-neutral description fits. Internal polyglot services with streaming are gRPC's home: one `.proto`, generated clients, HTTP/2 streams and deadlines. The dashboard shares a repo and a language with its server, which is exactly tRPC's condition. tRPC can't serve Go or merchants; gRPC would push merchants (and browsers) through gRPC-Web proxies.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL response arrives with HTTP `200` and a body containing both `data` and an `errors` array. What happened?

options.text: Partial success: some fields resolved and some failed — the client must check `errors` even on a `2xx`
The whole operation failed; `data` is a leftover from a cache
A server bug — any error must produce a `5xx`
The server is asking the client to retry

questions.explanation: GraphQL resolves fields independently, so one query can partly succeed. graphql.org's guidance is a `2xx` whenever `data` is present and non-null, "since HTTP does not yet have a status code representing partial success". Errors that stop execution entirely (such as validation) come without `data`. Clients that only check `res.ok` silently drop the failed fields.

prompts.prompt: Make `WatchOrders` a server-streaming call, and retire the deleted `note` field's number for good.
prompts.explanation: `returns (stream X)` makes the server send a sequence of messages on one call. `reserved 2;` stops anyone reusing a number that deployed binaries still associate with the old field.

prompts.prompt: Give the client the server's contract without importing any server code.
prompts.explanation: `import type` is erased at build time, so no server code reaches the client bundle — only the compiler sees the router. Passing `AppRouter` as the type argument is what makes every `trpc.x.query()` call type-checked.

prompts.prompt: One procedure reads, one writes. Pick the procedure types (they decide `GET` vs `POST` on the wire).
prompts.explanation: tRPC sends queries as `GET`s (input JSON-encoded in the query string) and mutations as `POST`s with a JSON body — so reads keep HTTP's caching and safe-method semantics.
